Hello, and welcome to the Data Engineering Podcast, the show about modern data management. Your host
is Tobias Macy, and today I'm interviewing Jonathan Ellis about how to make the best use of human
time when agents are building the software. So Jonathan, can you start by introducing yourself?
Absolutely. I'm Jonathan Ellis. I started data stacks 15 years ago to commercialize Apache
Cassandra. I spent a long time in the space of distributed databases and the JVM, and now I'm
running a small AI startup called Brock AI, where I'm doing neither of those things and writing
native code in Rust through agents. And do you remember how you first got started working in the ML
and AI space? Basically, well, so I guess to back way, way up, I've always been attracted to the
idea that as engineers, we should be comfortable building our own tools and automating our own jobs
and making ourselves more productive, which is a philosophy that goes all the way back to, you know,
Richard Stallman and Emacs and the people before him. So one of the coolest things for me is that is
how AI unlocks that. Whereas five years ago, I would have said, oh man, like I'm spending my time in
IntelliJ and it's, what is it? Five million lines of code? Like it's a ridiculously large project,
very intimidating to make contributions to. And now I can say, hey, I really wish this feature
existed in IntelliJ. Go and code dive it, figure it out, come back. Usually I think this comes back
to our topic today. I don't think the right approach is to say, just go build this, but rather come
back to me and give me the top three options and let's discuss the pros and cons and go from there.
But, you know, any tool that I use day to day now, I can enhance and extend using AI in a way that
wouldn't have made sense from a time investment perspective before the advent of Gen AI. And so
Brock is, Brock is basically an extension of that, where I said, hey, there's a bunch of tools that
I think should exist and nobody's building them. So I'm going to go build them. Yeah, it's
definitely pretty remarkable. The unlock that has happened because of the speed at which you can go
from idea to delivery or at least prototype and the ways that that manifests in terms of an
organizational context where you're working in a professional engineering team can have a lot of
knock-on effects in terms of what people are doing and how they spend their time, particularly if
the engineering team predates the past two years. So people who have built up a certain set of
workflows and expectations largely around code review, which is part of what we're here to talk
about. And so because of the fact that writing the code itself is no longer the bottleneck that
shifts the bottlenecks everywhere else. And I'm wondering how you're seeing that impact the ways
that engineering teams think about their job and the work that they do. Yeah. And I think this is a
place where collectively as an industry, we have more questions than answers. And I certainly have
opinions and I think we're starting to stumble towards some of those answers. But really, I think
what happened and how we got here is at first, AI was accelerating the act of creating code
incrementally more and more with every new model release. But everyone was still just kind of
slotting that into the existing teams and processes. And it's like, oh, great. Jonathan's faster at
writing code than he used to be. That's great. And we don't need to change anything else, except
maybe he tackles, he goes through the backlog faster. But now we're starting to see as we've gone
from, oh, it makes code 50% faster, or it makes it 100% faster or 200% faster. Now it really is 10x
faster now. And it's still getting even faster still. Because as the new models come out now, the
number of tokens per second they're generating hasn't gotten faster for the most part. There's some
exceptions. But the task size that I can give it, like that's what's changed. So I can have 12 tasks
going now with Fable, and they're each taking multiple hours, sometimes multiple days. And that's
what accelerates the pace of code generation now is being able to parallelize that with less
oversight, not zero oversight, but with less oversight. And so that's what's just completely broken
that old paradigm of we're just going to keep using these human-oriented tools and human-oriented
processes. And so what comes after that? What comes now that code is 10x faster than it was, how do
we fit the rest of the software development lifecycle around that new reality? And we can kick it
off, or we can set more stage if you want. But one of the first things to go, I believe, is the
concept of humans spending time reading through diffs and doing code review the way we did three
years ago, even one year ago. Because that's just not a good use of time. And I can flesh out my
thesis a little bit more, or you can jump in first. Yeah. So just as a quick reference for
listeners, you wrote this blog post about the fact that it's time to stop performing code review.
I'll add a link in the show notes. And I think that one of the other interesting elements of this
point in time is that, particularly for people who have been in the industry for more than two or
three years, they have developed a certain amount of their identity and ego around the code that
they write and the way that they approach code and their various competing camps of what constitutes
best practice or idiomatic practices for different languages or frameworks or ecosystems. And so one
of the points of contention that I've seen in my own experience is people saying, well, the code
that the AI is writing isn't the way that I would have written it, so therefore, it's not good. Or
it's ignoring this idiom that I have spent a lot of time perfecting, where maybe instead of using a
bunch of if-then blocks, I put it into a dictionary so that it's more of a direct access or maybe I
prefer a more functional style versus imperative style. And so there's a lot of these details that
at the end of the day really don't matter, except for the case where maybe they have a performance
impact. And so that, I think, is another piece where the human element of engineering is coming
under fire by the AI because you have to just let go of that fact of, okay, well, maybe I didn't
even read the code. As long as the code does what I want it to do, that's the thing I care about the
most. And there's the trope that nobody's paying for the software, they're paying for what the
software does. And so why do we as engineers spend so much of our time bike-shedding or yak-shaving
about the way that you write your for-loop versus does it do the thing that the customer actually
wants? I think that's an excellent point and it highlights one of the gaps or the differences in
approaches that I've seen in the talented engineers that I've worked with when it comes to AI,
because I think it's much easier to come to terms with the things that you're talking about for
people who have managed or led a team of human engineers because it's to some degree, like there's
differences for sure. And I'm definitely not saying that managing a team of AI agents is the same as
managing a human team because it's not, but it is similar in this one respect, which is that if you
have a team of human engineers and your code reviews take the form of saying, you know, I disagree
with how you wrote this switch statement instead of putting it in a dictionary and matching on that,
like that's not productive use of code review time. And it just isn't. And so I think that people
who have been in the position of running those teams have gone through that adjustment of coming to
terms with whether the code is functionally correct is more important than whether it follows the
idioms that are my preferred weapons of choice. The other way that I've seen this framed a lot in
various blog posts and conversations in the community is that people are no longer just individual
contributors. Everybody has to become a manager, but instead of managing people, they're managing
agents. And so you really need to bring your level of abstraction up to the point of the product or
the feature and not the lines of code or the modules. And I think that one way that I've seen this
play out is that teams who do have a strong culture of doing RFCs and architecture decision records
as the initial step along the path of actually getting to that feature delivery are better situated
to take advantage of the current landscape that we're in. Because once you have that RFC or the ADR
or the spec that details, this is the thing that we actually want to build, then the implementation
becomes automatic because the agent has that shared agreed upon context. And I think that the point
of review just needs to shift earlier in the process where you need to get more people involved in
that design and debate of what is the thing that we're actually trying to build and why versus how.
And so as long as the code that lands can be tied back to and validated against the original design
document, then the human review on the code doesn't need to happen as you just need to be able to
have a way of doing that validation to show that it aligns with the stated goals. Two thoughts about
that. So first on the general direction, we're all product managers now, right? We're all, or I
think that we're being pushed in the direction where the value we add as humans is less on how do we
implement this decision versus what decisions should we make? What is important to implement next?
And so I think that developers who worked in an organization where there was a very stark line
between those two groups and the engineers just implemented what another team was handing down as
the decisions. I think that's going to be, the time where that's a useful use of human time is
drawing to a close. It's not completely gone, but it's limited. And there's a line of sight to where
it's like, yeah, that's, that's, you leave that to the agents. That's just what you do. So I think
that teams that already had more of a porous boundary between engineer and product manager and, you
know, the product managers are now implementing proof of concepts with their own agents and the
engineers are participating in design discussions. I think that's a much healthier place and they're
going to adapt a lot better. So spending a bit more time on the review validation and delivery phase
of the software lifecycle, there has been a lot of stake put in the role of the human in that where,
oh, you need to have a human looking at the code before it can go to production because the humans
are the ones that know whether it's going to work or not, or have that broader context. Which even
before AI increased the volume of code wasn't always true. True. Because if you have somebody do a
code review who hasn't worked in that code base before, that's not going to be very helpful unless
the purpose is purely for educating them on what that code is doing and how. But even if you have
somebody who is expert in that particular code base, they're liable to miss things or if they are
the expert in the code base, they're likely already busy with their own implementation and don't
want to have to spend those extra cycles on the code review. But there's still the element of some
sort of validation and guardrails need to happen so that we can have confidence in the code as it is
written before we put it into production because we don't want to be dealing with constant
firefighting due to buggy and broken code. And so I'm curious how you're seeing teams address that
angle of what are those checks and guardrails that we need to put in place so that we can
confidently remove humans from that phase of the life cycle. So this is where that article that I
wrote that you mentioned was becomes controversial because for reasons that I don't completely
understand. When I say like I did just now, you know, a year from now or two years from now, humans
just won't be writing code by hand anymore. Most people look at the, you know, the curve that we've
been writing for the last two years and say, yeah, I can see how if I draw that line out a little
bit more, that's probably what's going to happen. But then when I say, and you shouldn't be
reviewing it either. And then they're like, oh, like just heads exploding. People feel very, very
strongly that, that, you know, like you said, code should not be pushed to production without a
human reading at first. And part of the research that I did for that article was looking at, like,
if you actually study this and measure it, how many defects do, does human code review find? And,
and the answer is typically about 30% of the defects. And, you know, if it's a more complicated
problem domain, like security, it's more like 20%. So humans aren't really good at doing code review
from a standpoint of, is this, you know, am I finding the defaults, the defects? And so I think the
reason why people have that reaction of, oh, I couldn't even dream of pushing this without a human
review is that we all have memories of the times where we did find a defect. And so this is part of
like, you know, our, our human ape brains are not evolved to be statistically literate. Like
they're, they're really good at remembering, you know, exciting things that happened once or twice,
but really bad at estimating, like, was this a good use of time to find those defects, given all the
other times that I did review and didn't find defects. So my standpoint is not that code review
doesn't add value. I'm not saying that because like I said, you know, I can remember times I found
bugs as much as anyone can. But my standpoint is that the time invested to find those defects is no
longer worth it and should be spent. There are higher value ways to spend that time now. Even if I'm
saying I need to spend 30% of my time or 50% or 80% of my time doing quality assurance or in the
literal sense of the word that I'm assuring the quality of the code, that it does what it's supposed
to do. Whatever number of time you think you should be spending on that class of problem, there's
better options than reading the code by hand. Yeah. Yeah. Just anecdotally, I'll call out that I've
actually got at least one production system. It's not customer facing, but it is team facing that I
have written entirely by AI and haven't read possibly any of the code. And it's been very useful and
helpful. So it's actually a project that manages the team memories and task and project graphs for
coding agents so that it's a shared flat graph that everybody can access and read and write to for
being able to break down the context into chunks so that you don't have to have one session that
runs for three days because you don't want to lose all the stuff that you put in at the beginning.
And also be able to have the memory be compatible across different agent harnesses rather than just
a random markdown file somewhere on your disk that you hope doesn't disappear sometime. And I've
also bypassed a lot of the human review element of it as well because it works. I use it. I make
changes. I make sure that the changes do what I want them to do. And then I ship it. Exactly. Yeah.
And I think that's kind of like the easy case, right? And I don't mean that disparagingly, but in
the sense that if I'm building an internal tool for a small audience where, you know, the world
doesn't end if there's a bug, then yeah, just ship it and use it and fix problems when you find
them. And then the more interesting question is, how do you do that in a situation where the world
doesn't when you ship a bug? Or like there's potentially very bad consequences if you ship buggy
code. And then how do we do that now? And I think that a healthy way to start that discussion is
from what I just said, that actually you weren't catching all of the bugs by reading the code before
anyway. And therefore, what does that imply for what we should be doing with that time that we're no
longer spending reading the code? And I think that one of the ways that we can spend that time is by
getting the agent to help with building those quality gates and validation loops so that you can
catch those errors early and often, preferably even before it gets to a PR. Where I think maybe that
ties us into some of the work that you're doing where I know that the Bifrost tool is a linter and
MCP server that gives a more comprehensive view of the code structure so the agent can have that
insight rather than having to rely on a thousand grep calls to find a particular symbol. And so I'd
be interested in hearing some of what you're investing time in on that angle and also some of the
other ways that you're seeing teams use the accelerated pace of delivery to put more of that work
into the CI systems and guardrails and validation cycles that we should have been building all
along, but deprioritized because it took too much time off of the actual product that we were trying
to ship. Yeah. So as you said, I'm building a tool called Bifrost that is the way I think of it is
it's basically Coverity, which is a static analysis tool that's been around since, man, I want to
say like 1996, like it's pretty old, but it's also, it's really powerful and it's really slow and
it's really difficult to extend. But what it can do is find things like a use after free, or it can
find certain classes of concurrency deadlocks by analyzing the flow of data through your program.
And so I want to bring that caliber of deterministic analysis into agent harnesses where it's not
like, let's push this and let's CI crank on it for a couple hours and see what it comes back with.
But rather the agent makes a tool call that says, you know, run the use after free checks and it
gets back an answer in milliseconds instead of minutes or hours. And so to do that, to make Bifrost
itself, which, so we're tackling 13 languages at once. And I think, I think, you know, there's other
tools out there, but I think we're probably the first one to try to do so many languages all at
once. And obviously AI makes that possible with the work parallelization that I mentioned, but
guaranteeing correctness is actually still really hard. There's so many corner cases when you have
so many languages that you're dealing with. And so one of the big technique or like the big idea
that I, that I orient my thinking around is I gave, I gave a talk not long ago where I talked about
your, you should be trying to build an Oracle for your agents and you should use agents to build
that Oracle. And of course, an Oracle is a term from AI engineering where we're talking about
something that knows the right answer for a certain class of problem. And it's usually because we've
constructed the problem in such a way that we know the answer up front or we can derive the answer
much more easily than we can in a, in the fully general problem space. And so categories of tools
that, that, you know, the QA engineering space knows about include things like fuzz testing,
includes things like property checkers. And so we've built for, for Bifrost, all of those things.
And, and we use that to, you know, let, let the agents triage the bugs that they find. So that's the
other thing that agents unlock, by the way, is that a lot of these techniques like fuzz testing
isn't new and, you know, mutation testing isn't new. And like all of these techniques that we use,
none of these are new. I'm not that creative, but what's new is that. You know, before AI, if you
had, you know, a, a, a, a sonar cube or a find bugs or a coverity or like any of these static
analysis checking reports, like they generate tons of false positives. And that, that's, that's just
the nature of the problem space. And so most teams didn't bother unless they were in an extremely
sensitive space where, you know, releasing bugs is just catastrophic. In which case, like the, the
investment of time to use these tools would pay off. But for most tools, and even at my last
company, even at data stacks where we're building Apache Cassandra used by companies like Apple and
Netflix and, you know, all of these other companies to store data that they cared very deeply about.
Even there, we only made minimal use of this kind of static analysis because like there's, like I
said, there's just so much false positives. But now you can just tell Opus or Sol or, you know, your
model of choice, go through this report and throw out the false positives and create tickets for the
ones that we need to fix. Like that, that unlocks so many of these things that, that software
engineering researchers have come up with over the last 20 years and nobody could use because we
didn't have the time to implement them or the, the effort didn't pay off. But now code isn't, code
isn't the only thing that's free anymore or very close to free. You know, reviewing the outputs of
these tools is also free now. And so now that so much of the work can be automated, there are,
there's always the problem of running around with a hammer and trying to hit everything that might
be a nail. And so I'm wondering what are some of the ways that you are seeing the best return on
investment for human time spent and how, what are some of the useful heuristics around what are the
places that AI is going to be most useful and most effective versus the time where I need to use my
own human judgment and reasoning, which also potentially segues us into the conversation of how do
we help people build up that knowledge and reasoning? If they're early in their career and haven't
gone through all of the painful learning paths of people who have been in the industry prior to AI.
Yeah, those are two, two very different topics, but, but both of them interesting. So on the first
one, how do you decide where to spend your time? I think, so for me, the best use of time has been,
like, as I mentioned, building, building more oracles and building the harnesses that to drive
those. And there, like I said, I'm not a super creative guy. So I just go to, you know, chat GPT or
Claude and I say, you know, the way I would start with a new project is I would say, hey, what are
some of the most interesting research approaches from the last 20 years of software development or
software engineering research that I could apply to this project? And, you know, order them by your
expected cost benefit and, you know, start figuring out how to build them from there. The other
thing that's, that's a good use of time is building better tools. So, like, you know, all of, all of
those things that I'm talking about, we have custom harnesses for Bifrost to, to drive those. It's
not just like type into codex, hey, do some differential analysis for me, but rather, you know,
we're going to build a, a system that can do that, you know, as a nightly job and then give me a
report and feed that through the agent that's going to triage it for actual defects and so forth.
And that can be at the, you know, since Bifrost is a tool for agents to use, a lot of what we do
involves looking through the traces of a model that's trying to use the Bifrost tools and then, you
know, figuring out where the tools were less helpful than expected. So, one of the very low level
things we built is something to parse codexes trajectories for the Bifrost tool calls and pull out
the appropriate context so that Astra doesn't have to reinvent that wheel every time it's tackling
one of these jobs. And at, you know, I've, you know, I've, I've created kind of a meta harness or a
harness harness so that I can use my codex and my Anthropic and my Kimi and my GLM subscriptions all
in a single pane of glass and keep track of what the different agents are doing. The other thing
that you mentioned was, was about how do you upskill as a junior engineer? So, if you want to take
the conversation in that direction, we could do that. Yeah, I think that that is an interesting
angle as well, because everybody's asking the question. Various people have attempted an answer, but
I haven't seen a, I haven't seen any sort of standard developed as far as what are the actual ways
that we do that. Not that we did a great job of it prior to AI, but now there are potentially fewer
opportunities or depending how you look at it, more opportunity because the junior engineer can get
more done, but they're also holding a bigger foot gun. So, there's potentially a larger blast radius
of poor understanding of the problem. And I think that one of the ways that humans can spend their
time and tying back to what you were saying about mining the agent traces for how the, how it's
issuing the tool calls for Bifrost or any other tool is that in order to prevent a lot of wasted
compute and tokens on retreading the same ground over 50 different agent sessions, as well as giving
junior engineers a place to look to understand what are the best practices or how do we tackle these
types of problems is through the introduction of different skills documents that helps the agent do
the work, but also acts as an artifact that people can look at to understand what do we, what is the
approach for doing this and why did we do it this way? So, that acts as a shared repository of
knowledge if you take the time to actually look at it. And that's actually another area that I and
my team have been spending time is every time I have to keep doing something a certain way, I say,
okay, great, let's go ahead and read back through all the sessions where I did this particular
workflow, codify that into a skill so that I can just trigger it when I want to do that thing again.
So, one example of that is actually for code review because I'll open a pull request from my agent,
I'll get a different agent to do reviews on that. Lately, it's been co-pilot, but whatever other
agent. And then I have a skill that says address PR feedback that we'll just go through, find all
the comments and pull them in, perform the necessary, evaluate, perform the necessary changes and
then close those responses. And so, that gives me a way to go back and forth on create the code, get
some feedback on it, address some of the problems without having to involve a human until after
that's already been done. If I say this actually is a large enough change that I want to have
somebody else look to make sure that my general approach and design is correct before I actually
merge and ship this. Yeah, someone, so for a couple years there, and I think we've broadly moved
past this point, but for a couple years, people were saying, well, the AI is like an intern. And,
you know, it's reasonably smart, but it makes a lot of mistakes and it kind of doesn't know what it
doesn't know. So, you've got to supervise it closely. And that was their mental model of the AI
agent. And, you know, now the agents are smarter and better at writing code, but, you know, they
still don't have the big picture. So, someone said, and I don't remember who, that a better model
now is, it's not an intern so much as it's a great new hire. And every time you talk to him, it's
his first day at the company. And so, what that pushes us towards is some of the things that you're
talking about that were kind of best practices already in human-oriented teams that, at least teams
that hired new people regularly, that you need to have this knowledge base and this, you know, a set
of runbooks. And things that let those new hires orient themselves to what's going on and what are
the decisions we've made that we don't need to relitigate every day. And, you know, what are, you
know, what's our big hairy goal, right? What are we trying to build here and why and what problems
are we solving and so forth. And so, the difference is, of course, that maintaining that was always
super, super difficult in the before times. And so, most teams played, you know, didn't do as good a
job as they could have. And now I can just say, okay, Fable, document what we did and the dead ends
we ran into and put that in a, you know, put that in our set of plan documents so that we don't have
to re-derive that next time. And, you know, we can talk about how I don't think text files, I come
from a database background. So, I think there's better solutions than a directory full of markdown
files. But that's kind of where we are right now is the markdown file level. And it works pretty
well. Eventually, you do outgrow it, but it does work pretty well, surprisingly well even for what
it is. And then, as a very tactical piece, one of the things that works really well for us is OpenAI
wrote an article almost a year ago now. I think it was in November of 25, but it was late 25. And
they wrote an article about using something called exec plans to drive agents for longer tasks. And
the framing of the article was, here's a structure for how to create plan documents and have your
agent create the plan documents that it can follow that will keep it on task over a task that takes
hours or days. And remember, this is back, you know, like Codex 5.1, I think, was state of the art
because 5.2 came out in December, and this was definitely before that. And the opus was around 4.5,
I think. And both of these models were the start of the new agent engage that we're in now. But they
both got distracted really easily, and they both were a little bit lazy where if you gave them a big
task, they'd do the first part and then stop. And if you just said, well, slash goal, do the big
task, then they'd go all over the place and compaction wasn't as good and so forth. So OpenAI said,
hey, use this exec plan idea to keep them on track across compactions in this longer running task
and so forth. And we mostly don't need plan documents for that purpose anymore. Or rather, doing a
slash plan in the harness is sufficient. But we're still doing exec plan documents because of this
category of problem where two weeks later or two months later, why did we do things this way? And
the exec plan captures that in a way that seems to fit how the agents want to work. A lot better
than trying to put it into a comment in the code. Because for a bunch of reasons, you know, the grep
and set approach to going through code means that they have holes in their knowledge and they'll
easily miss that kind of comment. But if you have a document that says, here's where all of our
plans live and go look at them if you need to understand why we did something, that works a lot
better. Yeah. And similarly for architecture decision records, this is the design and why we chose
to do it this way that the humans can also look at. And that's something that predates AI workflows
as well of humans who are joining the company afresh and they're working in that thorny corner of
the code and think, I know exactly how to solve this. And then there's, I've definitely seen tropes
of people saying, okay, every time you think you're going to solve this, increment this counter of
how many times people have tried to do that before going back to whatever it was before. I remember
that, yeah. And that's the way to be able to go from one to the other and also being able to have
memories that get superseded so that as you find out more things, you can have the most recent, but
you still have the way to backtrack to see what did we think we do at this point in time. And so
that's an interesting angle as well. Oh, so you should check this out. A couple friends of mine
started a company called Vectorize and their flagship product is called Hindsight. And it's
basically a graph and embeddings based memory for agents. So yeah, it is on GitHub. Yeah, I think
you should probably check it out and see. Yeah, at least there's probably some interesting ideas
that might be useful cross-pollination. And it might even be where you're like, oh, I don't need to
maintain my own anymore. I can use someone else who does this full time. Yeah, I'll definitely take
a look at that as well. And that's the other interesting aspect of the time that we're in is there
is a massive proliferation of people who are solving adjacent problems or maybe even the same
problem in slightly tangential ways where we're having an explosion of what are the different
concepts and primitives that we actually need for software engineering agents or agents for
particular workflows. And so it's the let a thousand flowers bloom mentality. And so it'll be
